metaDescription: Five compact cordless drills under $100, from an 8V mini to a brushless 20V, compared on size, torque, chuck and the limits you accept at this price.
expertTake: The DEWALT DCD777D1 is the compact drill to buy if you can stretch to its price tier, because a brushless motor and a name-brand pack make it the only one here that behaves like a professional tool. The DCA 20V is the value pick, pairing a high stated torque and a 2 Ah pack with a two-speed gearbox. If you only ever tighten furniture hardware and electronics, the 8V DEKOPRO does it at a fraction of the weight, but anyone drilling studs should look elsewhere.
introParagraphs: A compact drill trades raw power for a shorter body, a lighter pack and a tool you will actually pick up. The catch is that small size hides big differences in motor design, gearbox and battery that the box rarely explains.

This guide explains what a spending cap of $100 actually buys in a compact drill, what you sacrifice against a larger pro model, and which specs matter in tight spaces. Our top picks are listed above and the full reviews follow. Prices move, and the cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated.

products.name: DEWALT DCD777D1 20V MAX Brushless 1/2 in Drill Driver Kit
products.description:
The DCD777D1 is the compact drill with the most grown-up engineering in this price band. Its brushless motor replaces carbon brushes with electronic switching, so it runs cooler and spends less battery energy as heat, which is why a 2.0 Ah pack goes further than it would in a brushed tool. A two-speed gearbox and a 1/2 inch keyless chuck complete a package that can drive 3 inch screws and bore through framing lumber.

The cost is that it sits at the top of this roundup's price tier, and the single battery means you pause to recharge on big jobs. Against the Black+Decker brushless drill, which quotes 486 in-lbs of max torque, the DEWALT is the less showy but better supported option, because parts, packs and bare tools are stocked at every home center.

Upkeep is light. Keep the vents clear, store the pack indoors, and the brushless motor should outlast the first battery. Since the 20V MAX platform is broad, adding an impact driver later costs only the bare tool, which is the main long term argument for paying more here.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a compact drill that behaves like a pro tool.
pros: Brushless motor runs cooler and gets more from a 2 Ah pack
Two-speed gearbox suits both screw driving and drilling
1/2 inch chuck grips large bits and hole saw arbors
Stocked packs and bare tools on a broad platform
cons: Highest price tier among the compact picks in this roundup
One 2 Ah pack means a recharge pause on long jobs
No case, so bits and charger travel loose

products.name: Black+Decker 20V MAX Brushless 1/2 in Drill Driver
products.description:
Black+Decker brings brushless motors down into the budget tier with this 1/2 inch drill driver. The 486 inch-pounds of max torque is the highest figure in the roundup, though it is a peak number measured at stall, so it overstates sustained power. The single-sleeve metal chuck is easier to tighten with one hand than a two-sleeve design, and metal jaws hold a bit better than plastic.

The tradeoff is that the brand is aimed at homeowners, not trades, so the gearbox and housing feel lighter than the DEWALT. Compared with the DCA 20V, which offers 354 in-lbs and a two-speed gearbox, the Black+Decker offers more claimed torque and brushless efficiency, but fewer details are published on speed ranges.

Because it uses the POWERCONNECT platform, packs from other Black+Decker tools fit, which makes a second tool cheaper. Keep the chuck clean and store the pack at partial charge. The manufacturer cites up to 92 holes per charge for common work, a figure that depends heavily on material.
products.bestFor: DIYers who want a brushless drill with a full-size chuck at a low price.
pros: Brushless motor and a 1/2 inch metal single-sleeve chuck

products.name: DCA 20V Cordless Drill Set, 354 in-lbs, 2.0 Ah
products.description:
The DCA kit gives you the spec sheet of a much more expensive drill: 354 inch-pounds of claimed torque, two speed ranges up to 1500 rpm, 18+1 clutch positions and a 2.0 Ah pack. The 2 Ah pack holds a third more energy than the 1.5 Ah packs common in cheaper kits, and the maker says that is enough to drive many hundreds of screws on a charge.

The limit is the 3/8 inch chuck and the brushed motor. Compared with the Black+Decker's 1/2 inch chuck and brushless motor, the DCA is the more basic design, though its published speed ranges are clearer. Against the FADAKWALT 12V in this list, the DCA gives you roughly twice the claimed torque for a larger body.

Treat it as a household drill. Keep the chuck jaws free of resin, do not leave the pack in a hot vehicle, and replace the whole kit when the gearbox starts to grind. It has no wider platform, so buy it for the drill alone.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want the strongest spec sheet for the lowest outlay.

products.name: FADAKWALT 12V Cordless Drill Set, 21+1 Clutch
products.description:
A 12 volt compact drill sheds about a pound against a 20 volt, and the FADAKWALT uses that to offer 21 clutch positions with a top speed of 650 rpm. With 180 inch-pounds of claimed torque, it handles furniture assembly, cabinet hardware and small pilot holes in softwood.

The tradeoff is power. At a little over half the claimed torque of the DCA 20V, it will stall in a 2x4 with a 1 inch bit, and the low top speed makes drilling slow. Compared with the 8V DEKOPRO, however, it has more than double the clutch resolution and a stronger motor, so it is the right step up from a mini screwdriver.

The small pack means short runs, so keep it charged. Store the battery indoors, wipe the vents, and replace the pack, not the drill, when capacity fades after a few seasons.
products.bestFor: Light assembly and household repairs where weight matters.
pros: 21+1 clutch gives fine screw depth control for a mini drill
Lighter than any 20V tool in this roundup
180 in-lbs claim handles furniture and cabinet hardware
Includes pack, charger and a bit set
cons: Stalls in thick lumber and with large bits
650 rpm top speed makes drilling slow

products.name: DEKOPRO 8V Mini Cordless Drill with USB-C Charging
products.description:
The DEKOPRO 8V is a mini drill that charges over a Type-C cable, the same kind used by a phone, so you can top it up from a power bank or laptop charger. The listing says it is meant for wood and plastic and not for masonry or other hard materials, which is an honest scope for a tool this small.

It is the clear low-power end of the roundup. Against the FADAKWALT 12V, it has a lower torque class and far less clutch resolution, and it will stall in anything dense. Where it wins is size: it fits into drawers, car kits and toolboxes, and the forward and reverse switch doubles as a lock-off.

Ownership is easy. Keep the Type-C cable with the tool, avoid overcharging, and treat it as a precision driver for electronics, models and hardware. Anything beyond that and a stronger compact drill is the better buy.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A shorter body means a smaller motor and pack, and torque falls with it. The 8V DEKOPRO and 12V FADAKWALT fit tight cabinets but stall in lumber, while the DCA 20V and the two brushless picks keep a compact body with real torque. Decide by the heaviest hole you will drill, not by the lightest.

Brushless motors cut heat and waste less battery energy, so a 2 Ah pack lasts longer than it does in a brushed drill. In this roundup the DEWALT DCD777D1 and Black+Decker 20V brushless drill have them, and the DCA, FADAKWALT and DEKOPRO do not. If you drill weekly, brushless is worth the premium; for monthly use brushed is fine.

A 1/2 inch metal chuck grips large bits and hole saw arbors, while a 3/8 inch chuck suits household bits. The DEWALT and Black+Decker use 1/2 inch chucks, and the Black+Decker's single-sleeve metal design tightens with one hand. Plastic jaws on cheap chucks let bits slip under load.

The 2 Ah packs in the DEWALT, Black+Decker and DCA kits hold about a third more energy than 1.5 Ah packs. The 8V DEKOPRO charges over Type-C, which is convenient but slow for bigger packs. Remember that a compact drill with a small pack will force frequent charging on long projects.

Clutch steps stop a screw at a set torque, and two speed ranges let you swap speed for torque. The FADAKWALT offers 21+1 positions, the DCA offers 18+1 and two ranges to 1500 rpm, while the DEKOPRO 8V has far less control. For cabinet hardware, finer steps matter more than torque.

A drill on a broad platform reduces the cost of your next tool. DEWALT 20V MAX and Black+Decker POWERCONNECT both offer bare tools to add, while the DCA, FADAKWALT and DEKOPRO drills are stand-alone. If you will want an impact driver or saw, the platform alone justifies paying more.

specDecoder.meaning: Max torque is the force at the moment the motor stalls. It rewards short bursts and says little about sustained drilling.
specDecoder.watchFor: Black+Decker's 486 in-lbs and DCA's 354 in-lbs are peak claims, not like-for-like with DEWALT's description of its drill.

specDecoder.meaning: Voltage is the electrical pressure of the pack. Higher voltage allows more power for the same current, so larger tools use it.
specDecoder.watchFor: The 20V MAX label is the peak of a fully charged pack, nominally around 18V.

specDecoder.meaning: No-load rpm is the chuck speed without any resistance. It drops quickly under load, so it measures speed, not strength.
specDecoder.watchFor: The DEKOPRO 8V's 800 rpm and FADAKWALT's 650 rpm are low, which is sensible for small bits but slow for large holes.

specDecoder.meaning: A brushless motor commutates electronically, removing brush friction. It is more efficient and lasts longer.
specDecoder.watchFor: Brushless does not guarantee a strong gearbox, so check the chuck and housing quality too.

specDecoder.meaning: Each number is a spring compression setting at which the clutch slips, protecting the screw head.
specDecoder.watchFor: Position numbers are not comparable across brands, so 18 on the DCA does not equal 18 on the FADAKWALT.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor type and efficiency
howWeEvaluated.description: We began with brushless versus brushed, since it governs heat and run time in a small tool. The DEWALT DCD777D1 and Black+Decker brushless drill led this category.

howWeEvaluated.title: Chuck and gearbox
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared chuck size and material and whether a two-speed gearbox exists. The DEWALT and Black+Decker 1/2 inch chucks and the DCA's two speed ranges scored well.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and size
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered whether each tool is truly compact. The 8V DEKOPRO is the smallest and the 12V FADAKWALT next, with the 20V picks heavier but still short.

howWeEvaluated.title: Battery and charging
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared pack size and charge method. The 2 Ah packs on the DEWALT, Black+Decker and DCA ranked above the smaller packs, and Type-C charging earned a mention for the DEKOPRO 8V.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted recurring themes such as pack fade and chuck slip rather than relying on manufacturers' own claims. Unknown labels were scored cautiously because parts support is hard to verify.

howToChoose.subheading: Mini Drill vs Full Compact Drill

cards.label: Mini (8V and 12V)
cards.text: The DEKOPRO 8V and FADAKWALT 12V weigh far less and fit anywhere, which suits furniture, electronics and hardware. They stall in dense lumber and with large bits.

cards.label: Full compact (20V)
cards.text: The DCA, Black+Decker and DEWALT keep a short body but carry real torque, enough for deck screws and 1 inch bits in softwood. They weigh more and cost more.

howToChoose.note: Pick mini if you tighten hardware and never drill studs. Pick a 20V compact if a drill is your only drill.

rows: 2.0 Ah pack on a broad platform
Higher capacity at a low price

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A short front-to-back length, a slim handle and an LED to see inside cabinets. Tool weight with the pack attached matters over a long session.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The FADAKWALT 12V and DEKOPRO 8V are the lightest and smallest. The DEWALT DCD777D1 is the best compact pick if you need real torque in the same space.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You drill every week or want a platform to build on. The DEWALT DCD777D1 outlasts the DCA and FADAKWALT, and a higher brushless model goes further still.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You mostly fasten furniture and hang pictures. The FADAKWALT 12V or DEKOPRO 8V covers that, and the savings buy a good bit set.

maintenance.interval: After each use; store at half charge in winter
maintenance.why: Small packs lose capacity quickly if held empty. Storing them indoors keeps the cells healthy.
Compact drills have little airflow room, so dust raises motor temperature quickly. A puff of compressed air keeps it cool.
Resin and grit make bits slip. A wipe keeps small bits centered.
Brush wear causes weak power and sparking. The DCA, FADAKWALT and DEKOPRO are the models to watch.
A dull bit makes a small motor work harder. Fresh bits restore speed and extend pack life.

faq.q: Is a compact drill powerful enough for home use?
faq.a: For furniture, shelves and cabinets, yes. For framing and decking, choose a 20V model like the DCA or DEWALT, since 8V and 12V tools stall in thick lumber.

faq.q: What does $100 buy in a compact cordless drill?
faq.a: A 20V brushed drill with a 2 Ah pack, or one brushless model at the top of the band. You give up metal gearboxes and larger packs. The cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated.

faq.q: Are brushless compact drills worth it?
faq.a: If you use the drill weekly, yes, because they run cooler and last longer per charge. For occasional use, a brushed drill is fine.

faq.q: Why is torque listed in so many units?
faq.a: Drills quote inch-pounds while some quote newton-meters, which are the same force in different units. A figure of 19 N.m on the FADAKWALT is roughly 170 in-lbs.

faq.q: Can I drill concrete with these?
faq.a: No. None of these has a hammer function, and the DEKOPRO 8V's maker says it is not suited to masonry. Use a hammer drill for concrete.

faq.q: How long do the batteries last?
faq.a: Expect a few hundred charge cycles, or several years of household use. Store them at partial charge and out of heat to extend life.
